#20s

It can be tough to stay focused with so many distractions around. I’ve found a few habits that really help me concentrate more effectively.

By incorporating these into my routine, I’m able to get more done and feel less overwhelmed. It’s all about making small changes that lead to bigger results in terms of productivity and peace of mind.

#FocusHabits #Productivity

Phone scrolling addiction—often driven by dopamine-scrolling and variable-ratio rewards like a slot machine—traps the brain in a loop of anticipation and passive mental exhaustion.

Why It Happens

• Variable Rewards: Short-form feeds (TikTok, Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts) deliver unpredictable bursts of novelty, triggering small releases of dopamine with every swipe.
• Default Mode Network (DMN): Passive, low-effort scrolling keeps the brain's DMN active, causing hours to pass without conscious awareness.
• Negativity Bias / Doomscrolling: Chasing updates on stressful news activates the amygdala, flooding the body with cortisol and adrenaline.

Common Effects

• Mental Fatigue: Continuous processing drains prefrontal cortex control, shortening attention spans and impairing working memory.
• Sleep Disruption: Blue light and pre-bed stimulation suppress melatonin, while evening scrolling delays rest.
• Mood Impacts: High or increasing screen-use trajectories are linked to heightened anxiety, loneliness, depression, and elevated stress.

How to Take Back Control

• Change the Visual Environment: Switch your phone screen to grayscale and move addictive social media apps off your home screen or delete them in favor of desktop versions.
• Set Hard Boundaries: Establish phone-free zones (like the bedroom or dining table) and keep your phone across the room before sleeping.
• Turn Off Notifications: Silence all non-essential alerts to eliminate the compulsive check-reward loop.
• Use the 5-Minute Interrupt: When you feel the urge to scroll, pause and set a 5-minute timer, or redirect your attention toward physical movement or an alternative hobby like reading or cooking.
• Curate Your Input: If you must use feeds, actively prune them to feature calming or educational content rather than endless rage-bait or short-form clutter.
